QUESTION: Have you seen an unforgettable and beautiful view or scenery?
ANSWER: Well, one that still stays with me is the misty terraced rice fields in Sapa at sunrise: layers of green hills fade into the clouds like a living painting. I remember standing there early in the morning with the cool mountain air, and the sound of water gently flowing through the paddies; it felt almost magical. That view really left a deep impression and made me appreciate how breathtaking Vietnam’s landscapes can be.

QUESTION: Do you like taking pictures of different views?
ANSWER: Oh yes, I enjoy capturing different views quite a lot, especially when the light or atmosphere makes an ordinary scene look special. Whether it’s a dramatic sunset over the Saigon River or golden rice fields, snapping photos helps me remember the feeling of the moment. It’s not about perfect shots, but more about preserving that sense of wonder for later.

QUESTION: Do you prefer views in urban areas or rural areas?
ANSWER: I’d say I prefer rural views overall. The simple for this is that they offer a sense of peace and vastness that’s hard to find in cities. Urban scenes have their own energy with neon lights and bustling streets, but nothing beats the quiet beauty of mountains, sea, or open fields. Still, the contrast between the two makes both special in their own way.

QUESTION: Do you prefer views in your own country or in other countries?
ANSWER: Actually, I love views in my own country because they feel more personal and connected to my roots: iconic spots like Ha Long Bay or the highlands immediately come to mind. That said, I’m also drawn to foreign landscapes, such as the turquoise waters of the Mediterranean or snowy mountains in Europe, because they bring fresh wonder. In the end, the best views are those that make you pause and feel alive, no matter where they are.

QUESTION: What are your favourite activities?
ANSWER: Well, my favourite activities these days revolve around a mix of outdoor movement and creative downtime: going for long walks in parks, tending to my balcony plants, and reading or listening to podcasts in the evening. I also love exploring new cafés or street food spots with friends because they combine people-watching, good food, and casual chats in Saigon’s lively atmosphere. Ultimately, these simple pleasures help me stay balanced and recharge after busy days.

QUESTION: What were your favourite activities when you were a child?
ANSWER: Oh, as a kid I was all about outdoor play! Riding bikes through the alleys with friends, playing football or cướp cờ until the streetlights came on, and collecting random things like bottle caps or stickers. We’d also spend hours drawing cartoons or making up games with whatever was lying around the house. Those carefree afternoons felt endless and full of simple joy.

QUESTION: Did you prefer to do activities alone or with a group of people when you were a child?
ANSWER: Actually, I preferred doing activities with a group most of the time; it was way more fun sharing laughs, competing, and inventing rules together in the neighbourhood. Playing solo only happened when I was reading comics or drawing quietly at home, which I enjoyed too but not as often. Looking back, the group energy really fuelled my happiest childhood memories.

QUESTION: Are there any differences between the activities you liked when you were a child and those you like now?
ANSWER: Yes, quite a few: the childhood ones were mostly high-energy, physical group play outdoors, while now I lean toward calmer, more mindful activities like walking, reading, or plant care that fit a busier adult schedule. I still enjoy some social elements, but they’ve become more intentional rather than spontaneous street games. In the end, both stages bring happiness, just in different, more mature forms that match where I am in life.

QUESTION: Are there tall buildings near your home?
ANSWER: Well, yes, quite a few. Living in Ho Chi Minh City means I’m surrounded by modern high-rises popping up everywhere, from sleek office towers to new apartment blocks just a few streets away. They’ve completely changed the skyline over the last decade, turning quiet neighbourhoods into mini city centres with rooftop bars and constant construction noise. In the end, it’s a mixed bag: convenient for everything, but sometimes I miss the lower, greener feel of older areas.

QUESTION: Do you take photos of buildings?
ANSWER: Oh, occasionally, especially when the light hits them just right or there’s some interesting architecture that stands out. I love snapping striking contrasts, like an old colonial villa next to a gleaming glass skyscraper, because they tell the story of the city’s rapid change. Honestly, it’s not my main focus when taking pictures, but those shots often end up as nice reminders of how dynamic Saigon feels.

QUESTION: Is there a building that you would like to visit?
ANSWER: Absolutely! The Landmark 81 skyscraper here in Ho Chi Minh City has been on my list for ages because of that sky deck with panoramic views across the whole city. I’ve heard the observation floor at sunset is breathtaking, and it would be cool to see the architecture up close after admiring it from afar so many times. I think going there would give me a fresh perspective on how far the city has come.

QUESTION: Do you want to live in a tall building?
ANSWER: It depends, but honestly I’d be quite happy to; Living high up with a view over the city lights and better breeze sounds pretty appealing compared to ground-floor humidity and noise. Of course, I’d want good facilities like a gym or garden area so it doesn’t feel too isolated. All in all, it seems like a modern, convenient lifestyle that fits well with the pace of life here.

QUESTION: Do you look out the window at the scenery when travelling by bus or car?
ANSWER: Well, absolutely! I almost always make a point of staring out the window whenever I’m on a bus or in a car, especially on longer trips around Vietnam. There’s something hypnotic about watching the landscape roll by, whether it’s endless rice paddies turning gold in the late afternoon light or chaotic city streets flashing past in HCMC traffic. It’s my favourite way to zone out, daydream, and feel connected to wherever I’m going instead of just scrolling on my phone.

QUESTION: What are the most beautiful sights you have seen while travelling?
ANSWER: Oh, a few really stand out, like the misty mountains and terraced rice fields around Sapa at sunrise, where the fog lifts slowly and everything looks painted in soft greens and pinks. Another one is Ha Long Bay from the deck of a boat at dawn, with those jagged limestone karsts rising out of emerald water and the sun turning the whole scene golden. Closer to my hometown, I’ve had moments on coastal roads in Phú Quốc where the sea stretches forever on one side and jungle-covered hills on the other. It’s the kind of view that makes you forget time exists for a while.

QUESTION: Do you prefer the mountains or the sea?
ANSWER: It’s tough, but if I had to pick, I lean toward the sea just a tiny bit more: the endless horizon and the sound of waves, specifically that salty breeze always feel incredibly freeing and calming after weeks in the city hustle. Mountains have their own magic though, especially the crisp air and dramatic views from up high, and I love the quiet intensity of hiking through them. Honestly, I crave both depending on my mood: sea for pure relaxation, mountains for adventure and a sense of awe.

QUESTION: Do you like to take scenery pictures?
ANSWER: Yeah, I do enjoy snapping scenery pics quite a lot! It’s my way of capturing those fleeting moments so I can relive them later, you know, like a quick shot of misty rice terraces or a dramatic sunset over the Mekong. I’m not super serious about it with fancy gear, just my phone most of the time, but I love experimenting with angles and timing to make the photo feel as alive as the real view. It’s also nice to share them with friends or look back and remember how peaceful or breathtaking a place felt in that exact second.

QUESTION: Do you like reading?
ANSWER: Well, yeah, I really do enjoy reading! It’s one of those things that can transport me completely, whether it’s getting lost in a gripping novel or picking up random articles that spark new ideas. Living in a fast-paced city like Ho Chi Minh City, it’s become my favourite way to slow down and recharge, almost like a mini escape without leaving the balcony. Honestly, the more I read, the more I realise how much richer conversations and thinking become because of it.

QUESTION: Do you prefer to read on paper or on a screen?
ANSWER: It depends on what I’m reading, but if I had to choose, I lean toward paper for anything I want to savour, like novels, poetry, or non-fiction books that I’ll revisit, because the feel of pages, the smell, and the lack of notifications make it way more immersive. For news, blogs, research, or quick articles though, screens win hands down; they’re searchable, portable, and I can read at night without a lamp. In the end, paper feels special and intentional, while screens are practical for everyday stuff.

QUESTION: When do you need to read carefully, and when not?
ANSWER: I need to read carefully when the material is dense or important, like legal documents, academic papers, instructions for something technical, or even a really good literary novel where every sentence carries weight and nuance. On the flip side, I don’t bother with careful reading for social media posts, casual news headlines, product reviews, or skimming emails; skimming or scanning is usually enough to get the gist without wasting time. It’s all about matching the effort to the purpose: deep focus for depth, quick glances for speed.

QUESTION: Do you prefer scanning or detailed reading?
ANSWER: I prefer detailed reading when the content really matters or pulls me in, because a slow, immersive dive is where the real magic happens. You catch subtleties, connect ideas, and actually remember more. Scanning is my default for most daily stuff though, like browsing articles, scrolling feeds, or checking updates, since it lets me cover a lot of ground fast in a busy day. Overall, I think the best approach is being flexible: scan to decide what’s worth the deeper read, then go all in when it clicks.

QUESTION: Do you like watching team games? Why?
ANSWER: Well, yeah, I really enjoy watching team games. There’s something electric about seeing a group of people sync up perfectly, like when a football team pulls off a last-minute counterattack or a basketball squad runs a flawless fast break. The drama comes from the strategy, the trust between players, and those heart-stopping moments when one person’s mistake or brilliance changes everything for the whole side. For me, it’s way more gripping than individual sports because you get to watch relationships, chemistry, and comebacks unfold right in front of you.

QUESTION: Have you ever been part of a sports team?
ANSWER: Oh, sure! Back in secondary school here in HCMC I played on the class futsal team for a couple of years, nothing pro-level, just sweaty afternoon matches on concrete courts with mismatched jerseys and a lot of shouting in Vietnamese. I wasn’t the star scorer or anything, but being part of that little crew taught me heaps about passing the ball instead of hogging it and celebrating everyone’s wins together. Those chaotic games after school are still some of my favourite memories.

QUESTION: Are team sports popular in your culture?
ANSWER: Definitely! Team sports are huge in Vietnam, especially football, which is practically a religion here; you’ll see people glued to TVs or crowding street-side screens during big matches like the V-League, AFF Cup, or World Cup. Even badminton doubles and casual volleyball in parks are everywhere too, particularly among younger crowds and students. It’s not just about the game. Team sports tie into community spirit, family gatherings, and national pride, so they feel deeply woven into everyday life.

QUESTION: What are the differences between team sports and individual sports?
ANSWER: The biggest difference is the dynamic: team sports rely on cooperation, communication, and roles. Your success depends on how well you read your teammates, cover their weaknesses, and celebrate collective wins, whereas individual sports like tennis, swimming, or running put everything on your own shoulders, so it’s more about personal discipline, mental toughness, and direct head-to-head battles. Team games can be messier and more unpredictable because of all the moving parts, but they build stronger social bonds and teach compromise; individual ones often feel purer in terms of skill and focus, with no one else to blame or credit. Personally, I think both have their magic, but team sports just hit different when it comes to shared highs and lows.

QUESTION: Do you walk a lot?
ANSWER: Well, yeah, I try to get my steps in, probably 10,000 steps most days just getting around the city on foot instead of grabbing a Grab bike every time. Between dodging scooters, crossing chaotic intersections, and strolling to nearby cafés or markets, walking has become my default way to move. It keeps me active without feeling like forced exercise, plus I spot all those little street details you miss when you’re zooming by on wheels.

QUESTION: Did you often go outside to have a walk when you were a child?
ANSWER: Oh, definitely! We were always outside walking or running around as kids, whether it was wandering to the neighbourhood chợ for snacks with friends or trailing along with our parents on evening strolls to escape the heat indoors. There weren’t as many screens back then, so walking was just what we did to burn energy, play games in the alleys, or chase after ice-cream carts ringing their bells. Those aimless walks felt endless and full of adventure, you know, like the whole block was our playground.

QUESTION: Why do people like to walk in parks?
ANSWER: People flock to parks for walks because they offer that rare combo of fresh air, green space, and a break from the urban grind, especially in a buzzing city like Saigon where concrete and traffic dominate. You get to stretch your legs at your own pace, breathe easier without exhaust fumes, and watch other people living their lives, from tai chi groups to kids flying kites, which somehow feels both peaceful and alive. It’s also one of the few free, no-pressure ways to clear your head, get some vitamin D, and feel a bit more connected to nature in the middle of everything.

QUESTION: Where would you like to take a long walk if you had the chance?
ANSWER: If I could pick anywhere right now, I’d love a long, leisurely walk along the Cinque Terre coastal path in Italy: those colourful villages perched on cliffs, the turquoise sea crashing below, and narrow trails winding through vineyards and lemon groves sound like pure bliss. Closer to home, though, I’d jump at the chance to hike the full loop around Hồ Tây in Hanoi on a crisp morning, with the lake sparkling and fewer crowds than the touristy spots. Either way, somewhere with stunning views, a gentle breeze, and no rush; just me, good shoes, and hours to let my mind wander.

QUESTION: Where did you go for a walk lately?
ANSWER: Lately, I’ve been walking around Tao Đàn Park most weekends. It’s right in the heart of District 1, so it’s easy to reach, and early mornings there are magical with the big old trees, people doing exercise, and that soft light filtering through the leaves. Last time I went, I just grabbed a cà phê sữa đá from a vendor, looped the paths slowly and sat on a bench people-watching for a while. Nothing fancy, but it’s become my little reset spot that leaves me feeling recharged and ready to tackle the week.

QUESTION: What did you often do with your friends in your childhood?
ANSWER: Well, back in primary school, we spent most afternoons playing “cướp cờ” (capture the flag) or hide-and-seek in the small alleys around our block, and laughing until our sides hurt. On weekends we’d pool our pocket money for a bag of iced chè or those cheap plastic toys from the street vendors, then race bikes or draw chalk hopscotch on the footpath. Those simple, sweaty, sun-soaked games felt like the whole world was just our little neighbourhood, and looking back, they were pure magic.

QUESTION: Do you have any plans for the next five years?
ANSWER: Yeah, I’ve got a loose roadmap. I’d love to level up in my career, maybe shift toward something more creative like content creation or community projects that actually make a difference in Saigon. On the personal side, I’m aiming to travel more within Southeast Asia, build a solid savings cushion, and keep nurturing hobbies like plants and photography so life doesn’t just become work. Nothing set in stone, but the next five years feel like a sweet spot to grow roots while still chasing a few adventures.

QUESTION: How do people remember each stage of their lives?
ANSWER: It seems like we tend to remember stages through a mix of big emotional peaks and everyday sensory snapshots. Childhood often comes back as vivid colours, smells like street food or rain on hot asphalt, and that carefree feeling of endless playtime. Teenage years hit with intense drama, first crushes, and rebellion, while adulthood gets filtered through achievements, relationships, and the quiet routines that suddenly feel meaningful later. In the end, it’s less about perfect timelines and more about the moments that tugged at your heart or taught you something lasting.

QUESTION: At what age do you think people are the happiest?
ANSWER: From what I’ve seen and felt myself, a lot of people hit peak happiness somewhere in their late 30s to early 50s, old enough to have figured out who they are and what matters, but young enough to still have energy for new experiences and fewer major regrets weighing them down. Childhood has that innocent joy, twenties bring excitement and freedom, but there’s often so much uncertainty; later stages can bring peace, yet health or loss starts creeping in. So yeah, that middle stretch where stability meets curiosity seems to be the sweet spot for most.

QUESTION: Do you enjoy being the age you are now?
ANSWER: Oh, definitely! I’m really enjoying this phase right now; there’s enough freedom and self-knowledge to make choices that actually feel right, without the pressure of “figuring everything out” like in my early twenties. Sure, adult responsibilities pile up and Saigon’s pace never slows, but I love the balance of chasing goals while still having time for spontaneous moments. It feels like I’m finally living in the present instead of always rushing toward the next milestone, and that’s pretty liberating.

QUESTION: What was your dream job when you were young?
ANSWER: Well, when I was around eight or nine, I was dead set on becoming an astronaut. Seriously, I’d spend hours staring at the night sky from our balcony in my hometown, imagining floating around in zero gravity and eating freeze-dried ice cream. I even made little “mission control” drawings with cardboard boxes and drew rocket ships everywhere, convinced I’d be the first Vietnamese person on Mars. It was that classic kid dream fueled by space cartoons and the thrill of adventure way beyond our little city streets.

QUESTION: Have you changed your mind on your dream job?
ANSWER: Oh, completely! Somewhere in my teens the astronaut fantasy faded as I realised the insane competition, physics I struggled with, and the fact that space travel still felt light-years away from reality. These days I’m way more grounded and happy chasing roles that let me connect with people and solve real-world puzzles, like something in design, content, or even community-building here in Saigon. Looking back, I think that early dream just taught me to aim high and stay curious, even if the destination shifted to something closer to home and heart.

QUESTION: Have you ever had an experience where you did something well?
ANSWER: Oh yeah, one that still makes me smile was last year when I organised a small team-building event for my colleagues here. To be more specific, I turned a boring Friday afternoon into a rooftop scavenger hunt with local street food prizes and silly challenges. Everything clicked: timing, weather, even the shyest people got involved and laughed the whole time. Seeing everyone leave buzzing and saying it was the best work break they’d had in ages felt like pure gold! I knew I’d pulled it off really well.

QUESTION: Have you ever had an experience where your teacher thought you did a good job?
ANSWER: Definitely! Back in secondary school, I wrote an essay for English class comparing two Vietnamese folk tales to modern short films, and my teacher actually read parts of it aloud to the whole class because she said it showed real insight and creativity. She even wrote a long note on the front saying it was one of the best pieces she’d seen that year and stuck a little star sticker on it, which felt huge at the time. That moment really boosted my confidence in writing and made me realise putting thought and personality into something could actually stand out.

QUESTION: Do you often visit museums?
ANSWER: Not as often as I’d like, honestly. Maybe three or four times a year at most, usually when there’s a new exhibition or I’m showing a friend around the city. Life gets hectic with work and traffic here, so it’s more of a deliberate treat than a weekly habit. That said, every time I do go I leave thinking I should make it more regular because those little escapes really recharge me in a way nothing else does.

QUESTION: Do you like visiting museums and art galleries?
ANSWER: Oh, absolutely! I genuinely enjoy them because they’re one of the few places where you can just soak in silence and stimulation at the same time. There’s something calming about walking slowly through rooms full of colour and shape, letting your mind wander without any pressure to “get” everything right away. Even on busy days in Saigon, popping into a gallery feels like hitting pause on the noise outside and coming out inspired.

QUESTION: What did you learn from visiting museums and art galleries?
ANSWER: Well, one of the biggest things I’ve picked up is how much art acts like a time machine. It drops you straight into different eras, cultures, and mindsets without needing words. For instance, wandering through the Vietnam Fine Arts Museum here in HCMC showed me how wartime paintings captured raw emotion and resilience in ways history books never quite manage, and then seeing modern installations at the Factory Contemporary Arts Centre made me realise creativity keeps evolving with society’s chaos. Overall, those visits have taught me to slow down and look closer at every piece, whether ancient lacquer or bold street art as it carries someone’s story, perspective, or quiet rebellion.

QUESTION: What do you usually do during a break?
ANSWER: Well, during a quick work break I usually step away from the screen, stretch my legs with a short walk around the apartment or down to the lobby, and grab a glass of cold water or iced trà đá if it’s super hot outside. If it’s longer, like a lunch break, I’ll scroll through some funny Reels, reply to a few messages from friends, or just stare out the window at the crazy traffic—it’s oddly relaxing. Basically, anything that resets my brain without needing too much effort.

QUESTION: What do you like to do during a break?
ANSWER: Oh, what I really enjoy is popping in my earphones and listening to a podcast or some chill lo-fi while sipping coffee and people-watching from a balcony if I can sneak out. Sometimes I’ll do a quick five-minute meditation app session or just close my eyes and breathe deeply—it’s amazing how much calmer I feel after that tiny pause. Those little moments of doing almost nothing but something I actually like make the rest of the day flow so much smoother.

QUESTION: How often do you take a break?
ANSWER: Pretty regularly, I’d say every 60–90 minutes during work hours because I’ve noticed I get foggy and less productive if I push through too long. I follow a loose Pomodoro vibe—work focused for about that stretch, then five to ten minutes off—and I’m stricter about longer breaks for lunch or coffee. In the end, those short resets keep me sharp instead of burning out by mid-afternoon.

QUESTION: Do you take a nap when you have a rest?
ANSWER: Sometimes, yeah—especially on weekends or if I’ve had a really early start and I’m dragging in the afternoon, I’ll sneak in a 20 minute power nap on the couch with the fan on full blast. It’s like hitting the refresh button; I wake up way more alert and less cranky. During the week though, it’s rare because the workday rhythm here doesn’t really allow it, but when I do manage one, it feels like cheating in the best way.

QUESTION: Do you prefer typing or handwriting?
ANSWER: The former, for sure! It’s so much faster, easier to edit, and I can actually read what I’ve written without squinting at my own chicken scratch. Handwriting still has its charm for quick notes, journaling, or doodling ideas when I want a slower, more thoughtful flow, you know, like when I’m brainstorming something creative. But for anything serious or lengthy, typing wins hands down because my brain moves quicker than my pen ever could.

QUESTION: Do you type on a desktop or laptop keyboard every day?
ANSWER: Oh yeah, pretty much every single day. I bounce between my laptop for most things since it’s portable around cafés and home, but I do switch to a full desktop setup with a mechanical keyboard when I’m grinding out longer work sessions or coding. The tactile click of a good mechanical board just feels satisfying, like it keeps my fingers happy during long stretches. Honestly, I can’t imagine a day without tapping away on one or the other anymore.

QUESTION: When did you learn how to type on a keyboard?
ANSWER: I properly learned around age 11 or 12, back when schools here started pushing basic computer classes with those clunky typing programs that made you race against the clock to hit keys like “asdf”. Before that I was just pecking with two fingers like most kids, but once I got the hang of touch typing it felt like unlocking a superpower. By high school I was flying across the keyboard, and it’s been second nature ever since.

QUESTION: How do you improve your typing?
ANSWER: Honestly, I’ve mostly plateaued now, but when I wanted to get faster I used free online tools like Keybr or TypingClub for a few weeks, focusing on accuracy first then speed drills—those random word generators really force you out of bad habits. I also switched to a proper ergonomic layout and mechanical keyboard, which helped my fingers move more naturally without strain. At this point, it’s less about drills and more about consistency; the more I type daily, the smoother and quicker it gets without even thinking about it.

QUESTION: Do you like quiet or noisy places?
ANSWER: Well, I definitely lean toward quiet places most of the time—they give me space to think, recharge, and actually hear my own thoughts without everything competing for attention. Noisy spots can be fun in short bursts, like a lively night market here in Ho Chi Minh City where the energy is electric, but after a while the constant buzz starts to drain me. In the end, quiet feels like a luxury I crave more as life gets busier.

QUESTION: Would you like to go to quiet or noisy places on weekends when you are free?
ANSWER: On weekends, I’d much rather head to a quiet spot if I’m truly free—like a peaceful café tucked away in Ben Thanh Ward, a morning walk in Tao Dan Park before the crowds arrive, or just chilling at home with the windows open and no agenda. Noisy places are great when I’m in the mood to meet friends or soak up the city vibe, but for proper downtime I choose calm over chaos every time. It’s the kind of reset that makes Monday feel way less daunting.

QUESTION: Do you keep plants?
ANSWER: Well, yes, of course! I’ve got a couple of low-maintenance ones thriving on my balcony here in Ho Chi Minh City, like a resilient snake plant and some pothos that just keep trailing happily no matter how much I forget to water them. They bring a bit of green calm to the concrete jungle vibe of the city, and honestly, seeing new leaves pop up feels like a tiny win every week. It’s turned into a quiet habit I really look forward to tending.

QUESTION: Have you ever had a plant?
ANSWER: Oh, definitely—my first real one was a little lucky bamboo I got as a housewarming gift years ago, and somehow it’s still kicking in a corner of my living room. I’ve killed a few succulents along the way, mostly from over-loving them with water, but each flop taught me something about balance. These days I stick to tougher types so I don’t end up with a plant graveyard again.

QUESTION: What plants did you grow when you were younger?
ANSWER: When I was a kid, my mom had us growing mung bean sprouts in old yogurt jars on the windowsill—super simple, just soak, rinse, and watch them shoot up in a few days for fresh salads. We also tried cherry tomatoes in plastic pots on the balcony; they never got huge, but picking those little red ones straight off the vine felt like magic. Those early experiments sparked my curiosity about growing stuff, even if most of it was more chaotic than successful.

QUESTION: Do people in your country send plants as gifts?
ANSWER: Yeah, quite often actually. Plants are a really popular gift here, especially for housewarmings, Tet holidays, or new office openings, because they symbolize good luck, growth, and prosperity. You’ll see people giving money plants, orchids, or bonsai. Things like the kim tiền (money tree) are super common since the name itself carries that prosperous vibe. It’s way more thoughtful than flowers sometimes, because they last and keep giving that fresh energy to the space.

QUESTION: How often do you buy shoes?
ANSWER: Well, not that often these days. I’d say once or twice a year at most, usually when my current pair starts falling apart or I need something specific like waterproof sneakers for the rainy season here in Ho Chi Minh City. I used to be more impulsive, grabbing trendy ones on sale, but now I’m pickier and wait for ones that actually last. It saves money and keeps my shoe rack from turning into a chaotic pile.

QUESTION: Do you like to wear shoes that are comfortable or good-looking?
ANSWER: Honestly, comfort wins hands down these days. I’d rather rock a pair of cushy, breathable sneakers that feel like walking on clouds than squeeze into stylish but torturous heels or narrow dress shoes. Sure, a sleek look is nice for photos or special occasions, but if my feet are screaming after an hour, the whole outfit’s ruined. Life’s too short, and Saigon’s streets too uneven for sacrificing comfort just to look good.

QUESTION: Do people like to wear shoes that are comfortable or good-looking?
ANSWER: It really depends on the person and the situation, but I’d say most lean toward comfort these days, especially younger crowds who live in athleisure and sneakers 24/7. You see plenty of people rocking chunky, ugly-but-comfy dad shoes or minimalist runners because practicality rules in a city with heat, traffic, and endless walking. That said, for nights out or office days, a lot still prioritize the wow factor: Good-looking shoes can instantly elevate an outfit, even if they pinch a bit.

QUESTION: What is your favourite type of shoes?
ANSWER: My absolute go-to is white minimalist sneakers—clean, versatile, and ridiculously comfortable, you know, the kind you can wear with anything without looking out of place. Brands like Common Projects or Veja hit the sweet spot for me: simple design, decent quality, and they age nicely instead of falling apart fast. They’re basically my uniform for everyday life here—easy to clean after a sudden downpour and always ready for whatever the day brings.

QUESTION: When you go out, what do you carry with you?
ANSWER: Well, the essentials never change much: I always have my phone, wallet with cards and a bit of cash just in case, keys, and usually a small backpack or crossbody bag. I toss in earphones for music or calls, a reusable water bottle because hydration is non-negotiable in Ho Chi Minh City heat, and maybe a lip balm or hand sanitizer for quick fixes. It’s basically my mini survival kit that keeps me ready for whatever the day throws at me.

QUESTION: When you go to different places, do you carry different kinds of things?
ANSWER: Yeah, it definitely shifts depending on where I’m headed. For a quick coffee run or market trip, it’s super light with just a phone and wallet, but if I’m meeting friends for dinner or heading to a co-working space, I’ll pack my laptop, charger, and maybe a notebook. Longer outings like a weekend trip to the park or catching a show mean extra stuff: sunglasses, a light jacket for air-conditioned spots, and snacks to avoid hangry moments. You know, it’s all about matching the load to the vibe of the place so I’m not lugging unnecessary weight around.

QUESTION: What is the difference between the things you carry in the evening and in the morning?
ANSWER: In the morning I tend to go heavier because the day feels full of potential—I’ll have my work laptop if I’m heading to the office, a bigger water bottle, maybe breakfast on the go like a sandwich, and even an umbrella since Saigon rain can sneak up fast. By evening, though, I strip it down to the bare minimum: just phone, wallet, keys, and maybe a small power bank if I’ve been out all day. The switch happens because mornings are about being prepared for everything, while evenings are more about winding down and getting home light and easy.

QUESTION: Do you like modern art or traditional art?

Additionally, agricultural activities, such as burning crop residues, further exacerbate the problem, especially during certain seasons.

Firstly, implementing stricter regulations and standards for vehicle emissions and industrial pollution can help reduce the release of harmful pollutants into the air. Lastly, raising awareness among the public about the importance of reducing air pollution and adopting sustainable practices is crucial for fostering community engagement and collective action.
Overall, addressing the issue of air pollution in Hanoi requires a multifaceted approach involving government regulations, technological advancements, public transportation initiatives, and community participation. Let me tell you about a stressful yet rewarding experience I had last winter. It was finals week at university, and my laptop charger suddenly stopped working the night before my 10-page Environmental Policy paper was due. Panic set in immediately—all my research was on that laptop, and electronics stores had already closed for the night. 
Instead of giving up, I decided to investigate. Using a screwdriver from my desk, I carefully disassembled the charger’s casing and discovered the issue: a frayed wire near the DC jack had completely snapped. Remembering my brother’s hobby of building circuit boards, I rushed to his room and borrowed his soldering iron. After three shaky attempts (I’d never soldered before!), I managed to reconnect the wire. The charger sparked alarmingly when I first plugged it in, but miraculously, it worked!
This makeshift solution got me through the night. I submitted my paper on time and even got an A-. More importantly, it taught me two life lessons: first, that resourcefulness in crisis matters more than perfect tools, and second, that observing my brother’s tinkering for years had subconsciously taught me problem-solving skills I didn’t know I had.

QUESTION: What important decisions should be made by teenagers themselves?

Picking friends, hobbies, or even part-time jobs teaches responsibility; a teen deciding to tutor instead of gaming learns time management. QUESTION: Why are some people unwilling to make quick decisions?

QUESTION: Do people like to ask for advice more for their personal life or their work?

I think personal stakes feel higher, so we crowdsource wisdom there first.

QUESTION: Why do some people like to ask others for advice?

QUESTION: Do people prefer to eat out at restaurants or eat at home during the Spring Festival?
ANSWER: Well, during Tết, or Spring Festival, in Vietnam, the overwhelming preference is eating at home. It’s practically sacred. Families spend days prepping traditional dishes like steamed rice cakes, braised pork, and pickled greens, turning the kitchen into a multigenerational assembly line. Restaurants do see some action, especially in big cities like Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh city for younger crowds or reunions, but 90% of Vietnamese still gather at home for the main Tết meals. Eating out feels impersonal when the whole point is ancestral altars, family bonding, and homemade flavors passed down for generations. I reckon home wins hands down for tradition and warmth.
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: What food do you eat on special occasions, like during the Spring Festival or the Mid-autumn Festival?
ANSWER: Oh, the spread is a feast for both stomach and soul! When it comes to the Spring Festival, we could never miss out on bánh chưng and bánh dày! They’re square glutinous rice cakes with pork and mung bean in the middle. Their origins date back to thousands of years ago when a prince wanted to make offerings to his ancestors with food items that represented the sky and the earth. These glutinous rice cakes are perfectly paired with caramelized pork and or pickled onions. If you look at the Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are a must! They are baked goods with mung beans, lotus seeds or assorted meats as fillings, often come in a red box of 4 and are used as gifts for families, colleagues and friends. Every bite carries meaning: round shapes for unity, red for luck. I think it’s food as love, memory, and superstition all in one.
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: Why do people like to have meals together during important festivals?
ANSWER: Because meals withh family represent identity during festivals. To be more specific, in Vietnam, sharing a Tết tray of food on the floor or around the ancestral altar isn’t just eating. It’s reaffirming bonds, honoring the dead, and passing stories to kids. The act of cooking together, the likes of wrapping 50 rice cakes, builds teamwork; eating together creates equality. Everyone from grandpa to toddler gets the same pork fat. It’s also rare. Busy modern life means daily dinners are rushed, so festivals are the annual reset button for connection. I reckon it’s less about hunger and more about belonging.
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: Is it a hassle to prepare a meal at home?
ANSWER: Yes, but a cherished one, especially during festivals. Prepping Tết food takes 3-5 days: soaking rice, wrapping cakes, simmering pork for 6 hours. Markets are mobbed, kitchens are steamy, and someone always burns the first batch of mứt. But here’s the twist: the hassle is the ritual. Grandmas teach grandkids to fold bánh chưng leaves; uncles argue over salt levels. It’s messy, loud, and priceless. Daily home cooking? Sure, that’s a chore. Festival prep? It’s love disguised as labor. I think the effort makes the meal taste better.
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: What do people often talk about during meals?
ANSWER: In Vietnam, the dinner table is never quiet because it’s where the whole day is unpacked and relived. Someone always starts by praising the fish sauce or asking who cooked the caramelised pork, then the conversation quickly slides into school grades, office gossip, or whose cousin is getting married next month. Money matters slip in naturally, such as who’s saving for a new scooter, how much red-envelope cash to prepare, while parents remind everyone to eat more greens because “you look pale lately.” Before long, an uncle brings up politics or last night’s football match, someone drags out an embarrassing childhood story to tease the youngest, and laughter fills the tiny room. Plates get refilled, stories get louder, and even the smallest complaint about leaving the fish head for dad is delivered with affection. By the time the last grain of rice is gone, the family has laughed, argued, planned, and bonded all over again, proving that in Vietnam, the meal itself is only half the celebration. The real feast is the conversation.
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: People are spending less and less time having meals with their families these days. Is this good or bad?
ANSWER: Well, I’d say it’s mostly a bad trend, though not without a few silver linings. In Vietnam, the family meal has always been sacred (it’s where kids learn respect, elders pass down stories, and everyone feels anchored), so when people skip it for work, phones, or solo Netflix dinners, that emotional glue starts to weaken and children grow up with less sense of belonging. Busy schedules and urban hustle are real, but eating alone or in shifts often means more stress, poorer diets (hello instant noodles), and fewer chances to catch early signs of trouble like a teenager’s mood swing or a parent’s exhaustion. For me, the rise of separate plates and separate screens is one of the quietest but saddest changes in today’s Vietnam (worth fighting to reverse, even if it means just twenty shared minutes a day).
CONTEXT: Dinner Enjoyed with Family and Friends

QUESTION: How do children make friends at school?
ANSWER: Well, at school in Vietnam, kids make friends faster than you can say “Have you eaten?” It starts with shared space and routines: sitting next to someone in class, pairing up for group projects, or playing đá cầu (shuttlecock) during break. Teachers often assign seats or teams, so friendships kick off by default. Playtime is the glue: running around, trading snacks (a pack of Orion cakes = instant BFF), or bonding over who hates math most. Uniforms level the field: no fashion competition, just personality. By grade 3, cliques form around common interests (Pokémon cards, K-pop, soccer). I reckon it’s proximity + play = friendship, Vietnamese school edition.

QUESTION: How do children make friends when they are not at school?
ANSWER: Well, children often make friends outside school through casual encounters that feel totally natural. Neighborhood playgrounds or parks are prime spots, where kids bond over swings or a game of tag, sharing laughs that turn into playdates. Sports clubs or hobby classes, like soccer or art, let them connect with peers who dig the same stuff, building trust through teamwork. Online gaming or apps can spark virtual friendships too, especially for shy ones, though parents keep an eye on it. Family gatherings or community events, like Tet fairs, introduce cousins or neighbors' kids in a fun, low-pressure way. To me, it's this mix of real-world romps and digital dips that keeps their social circle growing without the school bell.

QUESTION: Do you think it is better for children to have a few close friends or many casual friends?
ANSWER: Actually, it depends on the kid, but leaning toward a few close friends often wins out for deeper growth. Close pals offer that rock-solid support, like sharing secrets or navigating tough times, which builds empathy and loyalty in a way casual buddies can't match. With a tight crew, children feel secure enough to be themselves, dodging the superficial chit-chat that comes with a big group. Too many casual friends might spread them thin, leading to shallow ties that fizzle fast, especially in Vietnam's community-focused culture. But a sprinkle of acquaintances keeps things lively, teaching social skills without the pressure. For me, quality trumps quantity. Those ride-or-die friends shape a kid's heart more than a crowd ever could.

QUESTION: Do you think a child's relationship with friends can be replaced by that with parents or other family members?
ANSWER: Well, not at all. Friends fill a unique spot that family just can't quite touch. Peers offer that equal footing for venting or goofing off, without the parental judgment or hierarchy that comes with mom or dad. Family bonds are about guidance and roots, like elders sharing Tet stories, but friends bring fresh perspectives and independence, helping kids carve their own identity. Sure, siblings or cousins can play a buddy role, especially in close-knit Vietnamese homes, but they still carry that blood-tie baggage. Relying solely on family might stunt social skills, leaving kids awkward in the wider world. To me, it's like comparing roots to wings. Family grounds you, but friends help you soar.

QUESTION: What are the differences between friends made inside and outside the workplace?
ANSWER: Well, friends from work often start with shared gripes about deadlines or bosses, but they can fade once the job ends. Inside the office, bonds form fast over coffee breaks or team projects, blending professional respect with inside jokes, though competition might sneak in and sour things. Outside work, friends are picked purely for vibes, like meeting at a Hanoi café or a soccer match, free from hierarchy or performance pressure. Workplace pals know your 9-to-5 side, making chats practical but sometimes shallow; external ones see the real you, weekend warrior style. The catch is, mixing the two can get messy if a promotion strains the tie. For me, it's like layers. Work friends add convenience, but outside ones bring the depth.

QUESTION: Do you think it's possible for bosses and their employees to become friends?
ANSWER: Honestly, yeah, but it's a tightrope walk that needs boundaries to avoid slips. A boss-employee duo can bond over shared hobbies, like weekend badminton or debating Vietnamese coffee spots, turning respect into genuine rapport. In Vietnam's hierarchical culture, though, power dynamics linger. Employees might hold back opinions, fearing favoritism or backlash. True friendship thrives on equality, which a pay gap or authority can skew, leading to awkward favors or resentment. Still, some pull it off post-promotion or after leaving the job, when the scales balance. For me, it's doable with trust and tact, but rare, like finding a quiet corner in bustling Saigon.

QUESTION: What are the differences between young people's and old people's preferences in music?
ANSWER: Well, the gap is pretty wide and predictable: young people chase energy, novelty, and lyrics about love, rebellion, or flexing, while older generations lean toward nostalgia, melody, and emotional depth. Vietnamese teens blast V-pop, K-pop, hip-hop, and EDM: fast beats, auto-tune, and TikTok-ready hooks from Sơn Tùng M-TP, Binz, or Blackpink. Their parents or grandparents, on the other hand, still melt for bolero, red music (nhạc đỏ) from the war era, cải lương ballads, or classic Trịnh Công Sơn songs that tug at the heartstrings with slow guitars and poetic lyrics. Young ears want bass that vibrates in the chest; older ears want songs that remind them of first loves or motorbike rides in the 1980s. Tech plays a role too. Youth stream on Spotify and YouTube, elders stick to radio or old CDs. For me, it’s like two different planets orbiting the same family dinner table. One wants to dance, the other wants to cry and remember.

QUESTION: What are the benefits of children learning a musical instrument?
ANSWER: Oh, it’s one of the best gifts you can give a child. Science backs it up big time. Playing an instrument boosts brain development (improves memory, spatial reasoning, and even math scores), teaches discipline and patience (those first squeaky violin notes are brutal!), and gives kids a healthy way to handle emotions. In Vietnam, learning guitar, piano, or the đàn bầu builds confidence. Imagine a shy 10-year-old nailing a song at the school Tet show. It also sharpens focus in an age of endless scrolling and strengthens fine motor skills. Long-term, kids who play instruments tend to have better stress management and higher empathy. For me, it’s simple: thirty minutes a day with a guitar beats thirty minutes of Roblox for building a sharper, calmer, happier brain.
CONTEXT: Friends Who Are Good at Music

QUESTION: Do you know what kind of music children like today?
ANSWER: Today’s Vietnamese kids are growing up in a total pop culture blender. The top playlist usually includes cute, high-energy V-pop such as Amee, Đức Phúc, or anything with rainbow visuals. QUESTION: Do you think the government should invest more money in concerts?
ANSWER: Honestly, yes, but selectively. Big, well-organized concerts (especially free or low-cost ones for youth and families) bring huge social benefits: they reduce stress, boost local tourism, and give young artists a stage. In Vietnam, events like Hò Dô Festival or Monsoon Festival already prove that government-backed music events can draw hundreds of thousands and create jobs. The money also supports sound engineers, stage crews, and venues that otherwise struggle. That said, it shouldn’t be blank checks for commercial K-pop shows with insane ticket prices. It’s better to fund diverse genres (traditional, indie, fusion) and make sure rural areas get some love too. For me, smart investment in concerts is smart investment in mental health and national pride: just keep it inclusive, not elitist.
